newsitem.title: UK: Could there be a sex gene for social behaviour?.
newsitem.headline: Could there be a sex gene for social behaviour?.

text.p: Researchers said on Wednesday they had found evidence of a gene governing social behaviour and they believe it is affected by a person's sex.
They said the finding could explain why males are more vulnerable to disorders such as autism, which can be marked by complete social withdrawal.
Other experts said it also raised the controversial possibility that men and women may really be mentally as well as physically different.
David Skuse of London's Institute of Child Health and colleagues did their research on women with Turner's syndrome, in which all or part of one X chromosome is missing.
Sufferers are usually short, have incomplete sexual development and often have problems with social adjustment.
Normal females have two X chromosomes -- one each from their mother and father -- and males have one X and one Y chromosome.
Skuse's group thought people with Turner's would be useful for studying sex-linked genetic differences as the chromosomes carry the genes.

"Males are substantially more vulnerable to a variety of developmental disorders of speech, language impairment and reading disability, as well as more severe conditions such as autism," they wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.
The Turner's women's genes could hold clues as to why.

When there are two copies of the same gene, one copy often "cancels out" the other. When there is just one copy -- as would be the case for some of the genes in Turner's women -- researchers can more accurately assess its function.
Skuse's group studied 80 such women, 55 of whom got their one good X chromosome from their mother and the rest who got it from their father.
Those who got it from their father showed better social adjustment "with superior verbal and higher-order executive function skills", they wrote.
They said their findings indicated that some genes on the X chromosome are imprinted. This means they act differently, depending on whether they are inherited from the mother or the father.
It could explain why men who get their X chromosome from their mother are more vulnerable to autism than females are.

"These data indicate that there is an imprinted gene on the X chromosome that influences social functioning and related cognitive abilities," Peter McGuffin and Jane Scourfield of the University of Wales College of Medicine added in a commentary.
They said the findings raised controversial issues -- such as why women seem more prone to depression while more alcoholics are male.

"Throughout the second half of this century, with the increasing emphasis on sexual equality, there has been a tendency to play down the possible role of biology in accounting for psychological differences between men and women," they wrote.

"Now, for the first time, we have evidence about the location of a gene that plays a part in behavioural sexual dimorphism, challenging the prevailing belief that gender differences are largely culturally determined."
Even more controversial was the possibility that related genes could affect intelligence. They noted that social cognition was affected.

"Genetic research on IQ has often provoked hostility, not least because it has been open to political misuse. Nevertheless, the evidence is consistent and cognitive ability seems to be substantially heritable," they wrote.
